title: Analytica explicatio methodi maximorum et minimorum

deep.reconstruction:
Problem: make A = ∫_0^a Z dx a maximum or minimum, where Z depends on x, on y, and possibly on derivatives of y. The page is Euler's 'analytic' re-derivation, in his own notation, of the δ-calculus that Lagrange introduced around 1755–1762.

§XVI concludes the simplest case, Z = Z(x,y) with dZ = M dx + N dy:
- Each element Z dx changes by N dx δy, so δA = ∫_0^a N δy dx.
- Since δy is arbitrary, N = ∂Z/∂y must vanish at every x. This is the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations, used tacitly.
- The condition does not depend on the endpoint a. That is natural, because with no derivatives in Z the problem decouples into pointwise extremization.

§XVII treats Z = Z(x,y,p) with p = dy/dx and dZ = M dx + N dy + P dp:
- Write p = (y' − y)/dx, where y' = y(x+dx). Then δp = (δy' − δy)/dx.
- The difference δy' − δy can be read in two ways: as the increment of δy when x grows by dx (d δy), or as the variation of dy = y' − y (δ dy).
- Hence d δy = δ dy (commutation of d and δ) and δp = dδy/dx.

§XVIII extends this to q = dp/dx, r = dq/dx, …, taking dx constant:
- δq = d²δy/dx² = dδdy/dx² = δd²y/dx².
- δr = d³δy/dx³ = d²δdy/dx³ = dδd²y/dx³ = δd³y/dx³.

§XIX: because δx = 0, δZ is obtained from the ordinary differential by substituting dx = 0, dy = δy, dp = dδy/dx, and so on. This gives δZ = N δy + P dδy/dx + Q d²δy/dx² + R d³δy/dx³ + …, i.e. the first variation of the integrand. The next pages integrate by parts to reach the Euler–Lagrange expression N − dP/dx + d²Q/dx² − … together with the boundary terms.
errors: No mathematical errors. The step from ∫N δy dx = 0 to N = 0 uses the fundamental lemma without justification, which was standard for the time.
The constancy of dx, needed for the higher-order commutation formulas, is assumed silently here; Euler only states it explicitly in §XXI on the next page.
The Z(x,y) case is degenerate: N = 0 is an algebraic, pointwise condition, not a differential equation. Euler correctly notes that it holds for every upper limit a.

ideas.what: Variation δy at fixed x, with the 'principal' and 'varied' states distinguished; δZ obtained as a partial differential with dx = 0
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (1755 letter to Euler; Miscellanea Taurinensia 1762); Euler named it 'calculus variationum' in E296
ideas.where_published: E296 Elementa calculi variationum and E297, Novi Comm. Petrop. 10 (1766)

ideas.what: Commutation d δ = δ d derived by finite differences: δy' − δy read two ways
ideas.where_published: E296, E297; Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385)

ideas.what: Formulas for δ of higher derivatives, δq = d²δy/dx², etc., with all mixed orderings equal
Arbitrariness of δy forces the coefficient N to vanish pointwise
ideas.modern_name: fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations
ideas.usually_credited_to: used by Lagrange and Euler; rigorous proof by du Bois-Reymond / Heine (19th c.)
ideas.where_published: E297 and the Methodus inveniendi (E65, 1744) in discrete form

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-documented exposition of Lagrange's δ-method in the same volume as E296; all content is standard and well covered in histories (Fraser, Goldstine).
transcription_corrections: §XVII: 'vnde perficitur' is most likely 'vnde perspicitur' (long-s misread).
Otherwise the transcription matches the image; the catchword 'XVIII.' at the bottom of p.104 is duplicated before the heading on p.105.
